metadata.file_name: Test scores and economic growth  update and extension.pdf
metadata.title: Test scores and economic growth: update and extension

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This paper does not analyze microdata from PISA/TIMSS; instead it uses previously constructed cross-country test-score indicators from Hanushek and Woessmann (2012a) and TIMSS 1995 upper-secondary results, aggregated to the country level and linked to Maddison Project GDP growth. Because the unit of analysis is countries (not students), complex survey weights and replicate weights from the original ILSA administrations are not applicable in the authors’ regression setup. The manuscript does not report any use of ILSA sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures, consistent with a secondary, country-aggregated dataset. Analysts using the underlying ILSA microdata would need to apply the original ILSA complex survey design weights when recomputing country test-score indicators, but this paper’s reported estimates are based on the authors’ already-constructed cross-country measures.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not model student-level cognitive outcomes with ILSA plausible values; it uses country-level test-score indicators (average test scores and shares above/below OECD-referenced thresholds) and relates them to country GDP growth. As a result, PV-specific handling procedures are not part of the analysis pipeline. Missing-data handling is also not described because the paper relies on already-constructed cross-country indicators from prior work and reports only an outlier exclusion (Zimbabwe) rather than an imputation strategy.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used Hanushek and Woessmann (2012a) cross-country test-score indicators (constructed from international mathematics and science tests in primary and secondary schooling between 1963 and 2003) and Maddison Project Database per-capita GDP growth (1960–2016). Main specification excludes Zimbabwe as an extreme outlier; a robustness specification includes Zimbabwe. For the upper-secondary analysis, used TIMSS 1995 results for students in the final year of upper-secondary school, available for 21 countries, and regressed these against average annual GDP growth for 1990–2016. For threshold analyses, defined 'basic literacy' as scoring at least 400 points and 'top-performing' as scoring at least 600 points in the Hanushek and Woessmann test-score dataset, then used the shares of students meeting each threshold as country-level predictors.

main_findings.dataset_used: Hanushek & Woessmann test scores (international math/science; primary & secondary; 1963–2003) linked to Maddison GDP growth (1960–2016), country-level
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 1: Average test score coefficient 0.013*** (excluding Zimbabwe; n=49) and 0.014*** (excluding Zimbabwe; n=49) with Adjusted R2 0.80 in column (2); including Zimbabwe: coefficient 0.014*** with n=50 and Adjusted R2 0.65. Robust standard errors in parentheses; significance: *p<0.1; **p<0.05; ***p<0.01.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Hanushek & Woessmann test scores (international math/science; primary & secondary; 1963–2003) linked to Maddison GDP growth (1960–2016) data at the country level, the study leveraged Average test score, Years of schooling (1960), and Log GDP per capita (1960) to explain Per-capita GDP growth (1960–2016), finding that a one standard deviation increase in test scores is associated with about a 1.3 percentage-point higher growth rate (column (2), excluding Zimbabwe). This indicates that improving overall education quality (as captured by international test performance) may be a key component of long-term growth strategies, though the authors caution that the estimates do not prove causality.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 1995 upper-secondary final-year test scores linked to Maddison GDP growth (1990–2016), country-level (21 countries)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 2: TIMSS 1995 score coefficient 0.006*** (SE 0.002); Years of schooling (1995) coefficient 0.001* (SE 0.0001); log GDP per capita coefficient −0.009*** (SE 0.0003). Adjusted R2=0.37; n=21. Significance: *p<0.1; **p<0.05; ***p<0.01.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 1995 upper-secondary final-year test scores linked to Maddison GDP growth (1990–2016) data at the country level, the study leveraged Average test score (TIMSS 1995 score), Years of schooling (1995), and Log GDP per capita (1960) to predict Per-capita GDP growth (1990–2016), finding that countries scoring one standard deviation higher in TIMSS 1995 had about 0.61 percentage points higher annual growth over 1990–2016. This indicates that upper-secondary education quality may matter for economic performance, supporting education reforms that strengthen learning outcomes beyond earlier schooling stages, while still not establishing causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: Hanushek & Woessmann test-score dataset threshold shares (basic literacy ≥400; top-performing ≥600) linked to Maddison GDP growth (1960–2016), country-level
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3: Share of top-performing students coefficient 0.087*** (SE 0.024) excluding Zimbabwe (n=49) and 0.106*** (SE 0.030) including Zimbabwe (n=50); Share reaching basic literacy coefficient 0.018*** (SE 0.006) excluding Zimbabwe and 0.015*** (SE 0.006) including Zimbabwe. Years of schooling (1960) coefficient −0.000 (both columns); log GDP per capita (1960) coefficient −0.011*** (SE 0.001) excluding Zimbabwe and −0.009*** (SE 0.002) including Zimbabwe. Adjusted R2=0.79 (excluding Zimbabwe) and 0.64 (including Zimbabwe).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Hanushek & Woessmann threshold-based test-score shares (basic literacy and top-performing) linked to Maddison GDP growth (1960–2016) data at the country level, the study leveraged Share of top-performing students and Share reaching basic literacy (along with Years of schooling (1960) and Log GDP per capita (1960)) to predict Per-capita GDP growth (1960–2016), finding that the association with growth is much stronger for top-performing students than for those reaching basic literacy (about 0.87 vs 0.18 percentage points per 10-point increase in the respective shares). This indicates that policies aiming to raise the upper tail of achievement—while also ensuring minimum proficiency—may yield larger growth-relevant returns, though the authors emphasize that these relationships are correlational rather than causal.

data.outcome_summary: This paper updates cross-country evidence linking international education test performance to economic growth. It uses country-level test-score indicators from Hanushek and Woessmann (2012a) (international math/science in primary and secondary schooling, 1963–2003) and Maddison Project GDP per-capita growth for 1960–2016, reporting that a one standard deviation higher test score is associated with about a 1.3 percentage-point higher growth rate (Table 1; Adjusted R2 up to 0.80 in the main specification excluding Zimbabwe). It further tests upper-secondary quality using TIMSS 1995 final-year scores for 21 countries and finds a weaker but positive association with 1990–2016 growth (Table 2; TIMSS 1995 score coefficient 0.006***). Finally, it shows that the share of top-performing students (≥600 points) correlates with growth about five times more strongly than the share reaching basic literacy (≥400 points) (Table 3). The study does not perform ML and does not establish causality; it also relies on already-constructed cross-country indicators rather than student-level PV-based modeling.
